newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Seven accuses Optus of breaking deal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Seven accuses Optus of breaking deal.

text.p: Seven Network Ltd alleged in court on Monday that its fellow shareholders in pay TV group Optus Vision had intended to form a favourable deal with Nine Network which would have breached Optus Vision's shareholders agreement.

Lawyer Roger Gyles, opening Seven's litigation case against Optus Vision and the other Optus Vision shareholders in the New South Wales Supreme Court, said Optus Vision had intended to form a deal with Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd unit Nine Network, Seven's main rival.
PBL holds a five percent stake in Optus Vision. Seven, which has a two percent stake, has said that it would have the right to buy Optus Vision at a discounted price if it wins the case.

Gyles said the deal would have given Nine more favourable terms with Optus Vision than the arrangement Seven had with the pay television group. "We didn't want Nine to get a more favourable agreement," Gyles told the court.

He said the intention to form the agreement between Nine and the other Optus Vision shareholders followed Publishing and Broadcasting's involvement in the rescue of troubled satellite TV group Australis Media Ltd last year.
Australis also formed a satellite TV joint venture with Optus Vision, which is also 46.5 percent owned each by Optus Communications Pty Ltd and Continental CableVision Inc, a unit of U.S. West Inc.

Seven claims the proposed deal between PBL and Optus Vision is a pay back for getting Australis more closely aligned with Optus Vision. Australis has programming arrangements with Foxtel, a rival cable TV network to Optus Vision.
Foxtel is jointly owned between government owned telecoms firm Telstra Corp and Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd which in turn owns 15 percent of Seven Network.
"To be able to tinker with that (shareholders agreement) is a breach of the obligations that they have to one another," Gyles said.
Optus Communications said earlier that it and its partners remained firm in their belief that there had been no breach of the Optus Vision shareholders agreement, as alleged by Seven.
If Seven Network wins the case, which is expected to take at least two weeks, it says it would be entitled to buy the remaining 98 percent of Optus Vision it does not already own.
Seven, which is 24 percent owned by its chairman Kerry Stokes, has said it would on-sell Optus Vision to an overseas telephone company.
Seven's court action, through its subsidiary Tallglen Pty Ltd, has delayed the float of Optus Communications, Australia's second biggest communications company.
Optus Communications is 25 percent owned by Mayne Nickless Ltd and 24.5 percent each by BellSouth Corp and Cable and Wireless Plc.
Optus Communications said earlier that it had postponed financial results presentations scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday, citing uncertainty arising from litigation by Seven.
Seven shares closed four cents down at A$4.31.
